node.label: The Science Wars, 1994–2000
node.date_label: Higher Superstition 1994 · Social Text "Science Wars" issue and Sokal's hoax 1996 · The Golem in Physics Today 1996–97 · Impostures intellectuelles 1997 (English 1998) · A House Built on Sand 1998 · Pandora's Hope and Shapin's reply 1999 · Later reading: Latour 2004
node.description: A dispute of the mid-1990s in which scientists and philosophers charged science studies with relativism and hostility to science, and sociologists and historians of science answered them. It is taught here as a moment in the reception of science studies: most of the attackers were scientists or philosophers, not historians. Gross and Levitt's Higher Superstition (1994) went after what an SHPS editorial called the "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science", the Edinburgh strong programme among them. Social Text planned a "Science Wars" issue in response; Sokal's parody appeared in it (1996), and his confession attacked "epistemic relativism" in cultural studies. In Physics Today Mermin judged that The Golem showed "what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective", and Collins and Pinch replied that many scientists were "scientific fundamentalists". Sokal and Bricmont (1997; English 1998) called the strong programme "either a valid and mildly interesting corrective ... or else a gross and blatant error" and charged Latour with sliding from "Nature's representation" to "Nature". Historians of science answered: Shapin (1999) called the charge of hostility to science "malevolently misinformed", and Latour wrote that science studies had "added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it" (1999).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Attack: Gross and Levitt, Higher Superstition (1994); Sokal, "Transgressing the Boundaries" and "A Physicist Experiments with Cultural Studies" (1996); Weinberg, "Sokal's Hoax" (1996) and "The Revolution That Didn't Happen" (1998); Mermin's Physics Today columns (1996–97); Sokal and Bricmont, Impostures intellectuelles (1997; Intellectual Impostures, 1998); Koertge, ed., A House Built on Sand (1998). Answers: Social Text 46/47, "Science Wars", ed. Ross (1996); Robbins and Ross (1996); Fish (1996); Collins and Pinch (1996); Wise in Isis (1996); Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (1997); Jardine and Frasca-Spada in SHPS (1997); Schweber (1997); Krige (1998); Beller (1998); Latour, Pandora's Hope (1999); Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (1999). Clarification: Hacking, The Social Construction of What? (1999). Later reading: Latour, "Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?" (2004).
node.scope_note: A debate entry about the reception of science studies, measured through its texts. The texts read are listed in the source notes; several central ones were not. Higher Superstition was not read: its words are given only as its in-period readers (Edge, Jardine and Frasca-Spada, Sokal and Bricmont) quote them. Wise's Isis review, the Social Text essays, Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997, most of A House Built on Sand (read only in publisher abstracts), Kitcher's and Hacking's books and The Golem itself were not read. The Jardine and Frasca-Spada editorial is the only source for Latour's Le Monde wording; the same journal later printed an "Apology" by the two editors (1997, unread), so that wording should be checked before it is relied on. Pandora's Hope was read in a retyped copy without book pages. Sokal's 1996 confession named no sociologist of science; his criticism of SSK and Latour dates from 1997. Mermin was a qualified critic who later defended Latour. Jardine and Frasca-Spada criticised both sides and are not drawn as one-way critics. Hacking and Kitcher present themselves as mediators and are not drawn as critics. Haraway and Latour are treated as broadly aligned (editorial decision, 2026-10-14); Haraway is not drawn as a critic of Latour. The 2000 end of the label is a convenience: Latour's 2004 retrospective is cited as a dated later reading, and later collections (The One Culture?, 2001; After the Science Wars, 2001) are named but unread.

strands.title: Higher Superstition and its first answers, 1994–97
strands.focus: Gross and Levitt attacked the academic left's views of science, including "exponents of science studies" and the Edinburgh strong programme; Wise in Isis and Edge from Edinburgh answered them. The book is known here only through its readers, so its targets are given as they reported them.
strands.works: Gross and Levitt, Higher Superstition (1994); Wise, "The Enemy without and the Enemy within," Isis (1996); Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (1997)

strands.title: The hoax and Social Text, 1996
strands.focus: Social Text planned its "Science Wars" issue as a response to Gross and Levitt; Sokal's parody appeared in it. His confession aimed at cultural studies and "epistemic relativism", not at named sociologists of science; the editors, Fish and Weinberg replied or extended the quarrel in public.
strands.works: Social Text 46/47 (1996); Sokal, "Transgressing the Boundaries" and Lingua Franca confession (1996); Robbins and Ross, "Mystery Science Theater" (1996); Fish (1996); Weinberg, "Sokal's Hoax" (1996)

strands.title: The Golem in Physics Today, 1996–97
strands.focus: A physicist and two sociologists of scientific knowledge argue in dialogue over whether The Golem strikes a balance between nature and the social; Mermin later defends Latour against other physicists. Qualified criticism, not a call to refute the field.
strands.works: Mermin, Physics Today columns (1996, 1997); Collins and Pinch, letter (1996)

strands.title: Intellectual Impostures and Latour, 1997–99
strands.focus: Sokal and Bricmont turn on the strong programme and Latour (the immoderate reading of Kuhn, the Third Rule of Method, relativity); Latour answers in Le Monde, at the LSE and in Pandora's Hope that science studies is "not at war".
strands.works: Sokal, "What the Social Text Affair Does and Does Not Prove" (1997/98); Sokal and Bricmont, Impostures intellectuelles (1997; English 1998); Fuller's report of the LSE debate (1998); Latour, Pandora's Hope, ch. 1 (1999)

strands.title: A House Built on Sand, 1998
strands.focus: Philosophers, scientists and some historians collect case-by-case objections to constructivist work: Collins and Pinch, Pickering, Latour, Shapin and Schaffer, Merchant and Keller. Known here from the publisher's chapter abstracts and Sokal's chapter only.
strands.works: Koertge, ed., A House Built on Sand: Exposing Postmodernist Myths about Science (1998)

strands.title: Historians of science answer, 1996–99
strands.focus: Historians of science reply in Isis, SHPS, Physics Today, Physics World and Configurations. Some defend methodological relativism (Shapin), some fault the warriors' ignorance of the history of science (Krige) or of physics's own philosophers (Beller), and some criticise both sides (Jardine and Frasca-Spada).
strands.works: Wise (1996); Jardine and Frasca-Spada (1997); Schweber (1997); Krige (1998); Beller (1998); Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (1999)

coverage.basis: Surveyed through 2000 in the research of 2026-10-14 (evidence-science-wars.md), with one dated later reading (Latour 2004). Later work, including The One Culture? (2001) and After the Science Wars (2001), is not yet surveyed for this entry.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scientists and philosophers charge that the strong programme and The Golem leave nature out of the explanation of scientific belief (1994–98)
proposed_edges.map_label: Strong programme and The Golem attacked, 1994–98
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal, "What the Social Text Affair Does and Does Not Prove" (author's text, 1997; printed 1998; cited by note): "The extreme versions of social constructivism and relativism -- such as the Edinburgh 'strong programme' -- are, I think, largely based on the same failure to distinguish clearly between ontology, epistemology, and the sociology of knowledge"; he quotes Collins (n. 10) as saying "the natural world has a small or non-existent role in the construction of scientific knowledge", while allowing that Collins may intend a methodological injunction. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): most scientists "point out the substantial missing piece in this kind of explanation: Nature itself" (p. 79); the strong programme "is ambiguous in its intent; and, depending on how one resolves the ambiguity, it becomes either a valid and mildly interesting corrective to the most naive psychological and sociological notions - reminding us that 'true beliefs have causes too' - or else a gross and blatant error" (p. 84). Mermin, Physics Today 49:3 (1996), p. 11: Collins and Pinch "infer from these studies a seriously deficient picture of the scientific enterprise"; The Golem is "an instructive demonstration of what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective". Mermin frames this as a question of balance, not a refutation. Gross and Levitt (1994; book unread) are known here only through Edge (1997, n. 4), who reports that they name "the 'strong programme' in sociology of science associated with the Edinburgh school" (p. 25) and Bloor (p. 52) while listing no work by Barnes or Bloor in their references. The replies are the separate ssk → sciencewars edge. Two targets share this arrow: the Edinburgh strong programme (Barnes, Bloor, Henry), named by Gross and Levitt (as quoted), Sokal, and Sokal and Bricmont; and The Golem of Collins and Pinch, Mermin's target, which belongs with SSK's replication studies. No strand is set for that reason.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand: the arrow covers the strong programme and The Golem (replication), distinguished in the evidence note.

proposed_edges.relationship: Sociologists of scientific knowledge answer that their methodological relativism was misread as hostility to science (1996–97)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period replies in the sociologists' own words. Collins and Pinch, letter in Physics Today 49:7 (1996), p. 11, answering Mermin: "Many scientists, especially those who have become spokespersons, are evidently scientific fundamentalists. ... Where we sociologists think of ourselves as trying to gain social and historical insight into science, the fundamentalists see heresy"; The Golem is "about as inoffensive a social analysis of science as one could wish for"; they cite historical work on the slow reception of relativity. Mermin replied on the same page that "the rightness/wrongness axis is not a relevant dimension in their kind of sociological analysis of science". David Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (EASST web text, February 1997; read in a web reproduction): "A powerful group of American scientists, apparently for political reasons, have chosen to mount a vicious attack on those scholars whom they take to be 'flying from science and reason'. One of their prime targets is 'social constructivism'"; the Edinburgh group "has always maintained that reality plays a central role in what comes to be believed about it". Edge is not on the ssk roster; he is on this debate's roster. Shapin's 1999 defence of methodological relativism is carried by the science → sciencewars edge. Bloor's own reply to the warriors was not found; his 1999 complaint that Latour joined "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" is on the ssk → latour edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: golem_physics_today holds Mermin, Collins and Pinch; Edge sits in sciencewars/higher_superstition.

proposed_edges.relationship: Physicists charge Latour with sliding from representations of nature to nature and with misreading relativity (1996–98)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): Latour's works "contain a great number of propositions formulated so ambiguously that they can hardly be taken literally" (p. 85); on the Third Rule of Method, "Note how Latour slips, without comment or argument, from 'Nature's representation' in the first half of this sentence to 'Nature' tout court in the second half" (p. 85); his 1988 article on relativity "illustrates perfectly the problems encountered by a sociologist who aims to analyse the content of a scientific theory he does not understand very well" (p. 115), and "Latour's analysis is fatally flawed by his inadequate understanding of the theory Einstein is trying to explain" (p. 121). Sokal (1997/98, cited by note): "Latour has produced 40 pages of comical misunderstandings of a theory that is nowadays routinely taught to intelligent college freshmen"; Sokal in Le Monde (31 January 1997, author's translation): Latour "mixes up ontology and epistemology, and he attacks positions that no one would defend". Weinberg (New York Review of Books, 1996): "The objective nature of scientific knowledge has been denied by Andrew Ross and Bruno Latour". Dissent among physicists: Mermin (Physics Today 50:10, 1997, p. 11) wrote of the relativity essay, "I believe such attacks miss the point of Latour's essay". Steve Fuller's report of the Sokal–Latour debate at the LSE (1998) judged that "Latour won 'on points'". Latour's replies are the separate latour → sciencewars edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Latour answers the physicists: science studies "added reality to science" and is "not at war" (1996–99)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words where read. Pandora's Hope (1999), ch. 1, "Do You Believe in Reality? News from the Trenches of the Science Wars" (read in a retyped copy without book pages; to be checked against the printed book): "in this guerrilla warfare being conducted in the no-man's-land between the 'two cultures,' we were the ones being attacked by militants, activists, sociologists, philosophers, and technophobes of all hues, precisely because of our interest in the inner workings of scientific facts"; "If science studies has achieved anything, I thought, surely it has added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it"; "we are not at war"; and, of the other side, "a few disgruntled cold-war physicists". Earlier, as quoted by others: Sokal (Le Monde, 31 January 1997) reports Latour telling Libération (3 December 1996) that the hoax was "a clever joke" that thrashed people who deserved it but not researchers in science studies; Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) translate a sentence of Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997 about "A small number of theoretical physicists deprived of the fat budgets of the cold war". That article was not read, and the same editors later printed an "Apology" (unread), so the wording is given only as theirs. Fuller (1998) reports that at the LSE Latour "supported" constructivism but "opposed" relativism. Later reading, not evidence for the claim: in 2004 Latour asked, "Was I wrong to participate in the invention of this field known as science studies?", while refusing "to swear that I will never be a constructivist any more".
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: impostures_latour holds Sokal, Bricmont, Latour and Mermin.

proposed_edges.relationship: Historians of science answer the charge that their field is hostile to or ignorant of science (1996–99)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period replies by historians of science, read. Steven Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (Configurations 7, 1999), writing as "a historian and a sociologist of science": methodological relativism "implies nothing at all about epistemological evaluations or ontological judgments" (pp. 3–4); the charge of hostility to science or ignorance of it, "—when directed to the work of many distinguished historians and sociologists of science—now deserves to be called by its proper name: it is malevolently misinformed" (p. 11). He names no protagonist; his target is identified by its arguments, such as Sokal's challenge to jump from a window. John Krige (Physics World, December 1998): Intellectual Impostures "is essentially a political tract" and "lamentably indifferent to the history and philosophy of science". Mara Beller (Physics Today 51:9, 1998): "The philosophical pronouncements of Bohr, Born, Heisenberg and Pauli deserve some of the blame for the excesses of the postmodernist critique of science." M. Norton Wise reviewed Higher Superstition in Isis (1996; unread); Edge reports his charge of "a willful strategy of distortion and demonization" (p. 323). Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) criticised both sides and are not counted as one-way critics. Not every historian of science sided against the warriors: Margaret Jacob wrote against Latour in A House Built on Sand (1998; see the truthdebate → latour edge). Physicists also criticised historians' method (Weinberg 1996 on Whig history; Sokal and Bricmont 1998, p. 69 n. 88); that thinner charge is not drawn as a sciencewars → science edge. The arrow targets the debate as a whole: these historians answered the attackers' arguments (Gross and Levitt, Sokal, Sokal and Bricmont, Weinberg), not the respondents' strand in which they sit.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand: historians_answer holds the respondents themselves. The arrow answers the attackers (Gross and Levitt, Sokal, Sokal and Bricmont, Weinberg), who sit in other strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Selected constructionist and relativist positions within science studies attacked (1994–98)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts. Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997, §I, read) report that Gross and Levitt went after "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science" (the book itself unread). Sokal (1997/98, read) disclaims that the hoax proves "the whole field of cultural studies, or cultural studies of science -- much less sociology of science -- is nonsense", yet attacks "the sloppy thinking and glib relativism that have become prevalent in many parts of Science Studies". The Social Text editors (Robbins and Ross, 1996, read) say science studies and cultural studies had "been subject recently to so much derision from conservatives in science". Koertge's anthology (1998; publisher abstract, not her text) addresses the view in "Science, Technology and Society Studies (STS)" that scientific results are "social constructions". An STS reply in its own words was not read: the Social Text essays (Harding, Fuller, Winner and others) are unread, and Robbins and Ross wrote as cultural-studies editors, so no sts → sciencewars edge is drawn.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand: the attacks named particular constructionist and relativist positions across several parts of science studies. Sokal limits his charge to tendencies in 'many parts' of the field, and Koertge's anthology is known here from its publisher's abstract only. Not a field-wide indictment.

proposed_edges.relationship: Physicists blame an "immoderate" Kuhn for founding relativism about science, while sparing the "moderate" Kuhn and leaving him to historians (1996–98)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing), following Tim Maudlin, separate "a moderate Kuhn and his immoderate brother": "We have no objection of principle to the moderate Kuhn, and we leave to historians the task of investigating the extent to which these ideas are correct in concrete situations. By contrast, the immoderate Kuhn - who became, perhaps involuntarily, one of the founding fathers of contemporary relativism - thinks that changes of paradigm are due principally to non-empirical factors" (p. 70). Weinberg (1996) lists Kuhn, "as I understand them", among those who deny "The objective nature of scientific knowledge"; in 1998 he wrote that Kuhn's later conclusions "have made Kuhn a hero to the philosophers, historians, sociologists, and cultural critics who question the objective character of scientific knowledge", and that "Kuhn made the shift from one paradigm to another seem more like a religious conversion than an exercise of reason." Sokal's parody (1996, n. 2) cites Kuhn (1970) first among the "revisionist studies" it mocks. This is a critique of Kuhn and of his reception; Kuhn died in 1996 and did not reply. His own earlier rejection of irrationalism ("labels which I categorically reject", 1970) is recorded on the science → kuhn edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: The hoax and Intellectual Impostures attack postmodernist literary theory and French theorists' uses of science (1996–98)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal's confession (Lingua Franca, 1996) targets "the intellectual arrogance of Theory --- meaning postmodernist literary theory" and argues that "The recent turn of many 'progressive' or 'leftist' academic humanists and social scientists toward one or another form of epistemic relativism betrays this worthy heritage". His parody (1996) presents "Irigaray's and Hayles' exegeses" among its exhibits; in Le Monde (1997) he writes that among the Masters "one indeed finds Derrida and Lacan, Aronowitz and Haraway". Sokal and Bricmont's book (1997; English 1998) is built around chapters on Lacan, Kristeva, Irigaray, Baudrillard, Deleuze and Guattari and Virilio; those chapters were not read here, and the read chapters (pp. 49–96, 115–123) concern epistemic relativism in the philosophy and sociology of science. Richard Evans (1999) welcomed Sokal's work on Derrida and Lyotard as done "far more effectively and knowledgeably than I could ever hope to do". No reply from the linguistic-turn side was read.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The book's targets range across several language strands (deconstruction, signifier_subject and others); none is chosen.
proposed_edges.include_note: Deferred after review (Sol, 1.134 finding 3): Sokal's confession attacks postmodernist literary theory, and the parody's citations and the unread chapters of Intellectual Impostures do not establish a critique of the atlas's historiographical language entry. Restore only on a directly read, accurately scoped critique.

proposed_edges.relationship: Appleby, Hunt and Jacob judge the strong programme's relativism inadequate to historical and scientific truth (1994)
proposed_edges.map_label: Telling the Truth against the strong programme, 1994
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The historians' own words: Telling the Truth about History (1994), read in the Norton 2011 e-book, which has no print page numbers; cited by chapter. Ch. 5 ("Discovering the Clay Feet of Science"): the social constructionists "could not explain the way in which technical problems, or new natural phenomena like viruses, set whole research agendas"; the social insight "does not, however, underwrite the more extreme claims of strong programmers who have never offered an adequate theory to address the complexity of circumstances and situations that produce reasonably true human knowledge"; "relativism fails the needs of historians just as it skirts the possible existence of truths in science" (n. 24 cites Barnes and Bloor, "Relativism, Rationalism and the Sociology of Knowledge"). Ch. 7 calls social constructionists "once called strong programmers". The book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax. No SSK reply to it was found; Shapin's 1999 complaint that methodological relativism is "routinely misrepresented" (n. 6) is a general answer, not a reply to this book. Print pages remain to be checked.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The book names Barnes and Bloor.

proposed_edges.relationship: Telling the Truth about History assimilates Latour's laboratory studies to postmodernism (1994); Jacob carries the objection to the Science Wars anthology (1998)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Telling the Truth about History (1994; Norton 2011 e-book, no print pages), ch. 6 ("Postmodernism and the Crisis of Modernity"), quotes the claim that "'Nothing special'" and "'nothing extraordinary'" happens in the laboratory, attributes it in n. 9 to Latour, "Give Me a Laboratory and I Will Raise the World" (1983), and comments: "Latour calls himself an 'a-modernist,' but his position seems indistinguishable from postmodernism." Margaret Jacob, one of the three authors, then wrote "Reflections on Bruno Latour's Version of the Seventeenth Century" for A House Built on Sand (1998). Only the publisher's abstract was read; it says the essay "seeks to show how wrong-headed" We Have Never Been Modern is about early modern politics. That wording is the publisher's, not Jacob's. Moderate support: one sentence of the book, plus an abstract. No reply by Latour to these historians was found.

proposed_edges.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over relativism and truth: historians defending historical knowledge, and scientists attacking science studies
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Comparison only. The disputes overlap in time and in people but neither is a critique of the other. Margaret Jacob took part in both: Telling the Truth about History (1994) already criticised the strong programme and Latour from the historians' side, and she wrote for A House Built on Sand (1998; abstract only). Richard Evans, a truthdebate historian, cited Sokal approvingly in 1999 as having done "far more effectively and knowledgeably" what he had only touched on in criticising Derrida and Lyotard. The historians' book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax, and Evans endorses Sokal rather than criticising him, so no critique edge is drawn in either direction. The Science Wars concerned the natural sciences and their students; the truth debate concerned historical writing.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Thin. Weinberg (1996, read) defends Whig history of science against historians who "refuse to take present scientific knowledge into account" and Sokal and Bricmont (p. 69 n. 88) reject that refusal; Pinnick on Shapin and Schaffer, and Newman and Soble on Merchant, are known only from publisher abstracts. Not re-read; recorded in the science → sciencewars note instead.
Thin. Gross and Levitt on Keller and feminist cell biology (p. 139, via Jardine and Frasca-Spada) and Gross and Soble in Koertge 1998 (abstracts). Higher Superstition ch. 5 must be read first.

No STS reply was read in its authors' words: the Social Text essays (Harding, Fuller, Winner and others) are unread, and Robbins and Ross wrote as cultural-studies editors. The SSK replies (Collins and Pinch, Edge) carry the answer.
Not supported: Telling the Truth about History predates the dispute and Evans endorses Sokal. Drawn as a comparison (edge 11).

appleby_hunt_jacob.note: Chapters 5–8 re-read for revision 1.135 in a Norton 2011 e-book upload (Internet Archive), which has no print page numbers; passages are cited by chapter, section and note. Ch. 5, "Truth and the Consequences of Social History" and "Relativism Redux": the social constructionists "could not explain the way in which technical problems, or new natural phenomena like viruses, set whole research agendas"; "the more extreme claims of strong programmers who have never offered an adequate theory to address the complexity of circumstances and situations that produce reasonably true human knowledge"; "relativism fails the needs of historians just as it skirts the possible existence of truths in science" (n. 24: Barnes and Bloor). Ch. 6: Latour's "position seems indistinguishable from postmodernism" (n. 9: "Give Me a Laboratory", 1983). Ch. 7: "once called strong programmers". Ch. 8: "It is time to come out of the trenches." Print pages not checked.
